about: Emuthon (Emden) at the mouth of the Ems, 793 to 1066: one port. A draft for the user to overwrite, written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/emuthon.md and the spine. (?) marks what could not be checked.

ports.summary: In 793 Emuthon is hardly a place yet: a low rise of clay sods where a creek meets a loop of the Ems, a few plank houses of Frisian traders, sheep to the edge of the sky. It is the last landing under the Frankish king before the Saxons and the Danes, and this summer it is in revolt. A merchant comes for wool, grey cloth, cheese and hides, and brings what the marsh has none of: grain, timber, iron, querns and wine.
ports.seasons: New cloth comes off the looms before Easter, the wool at midsummer after the shearing, butter and cheese all summer, and cattle are sold on the hoof before Martinmas. From Martinmas to Easter the boats are drawn up, the marsh floods at every spring tide, and the people sit on their mound among the stalled beasts and weave.

history.text: King Charles takes Frisia as far as the Weser. The district of the Ems mouth, Emisga, is the king's from now on.
Liudger, a Frisian taught at Utrecht and York, is set over five districts east of the Lauwers, Emisga among them, and the island Bant.
history.source: Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.22 (ed. Diekamp 1881), through de.wikipedia 'Liudger'

history.text: Liudger builds the first chapel in these parts, of timber, at Leer up the Ems.
This year the East Frisians rose with the Saxons under Unno and Eilrat, burned the churches and drove out the priests. Liudger fled, and was back within the year.

About this year a ditch less than a pace wide is dug round the first mound, some forty metres across. It is the oldest thing at Emden that can be dated; the place was most likely founded near this year, by traders.
The law of the Frisians is written down, with its own fines for the land between Lauwers and Weser.
history.source: Lex Frisionum (keesn.nl, Latin and English); chronicle_793.json

history.text: Liudger is made bishop at Mimigernaford and keeps his five Frisian districts. The Ems mouth belongs to that see from now on.
On the twenty-sixth of March Liudger dies.
This year two hundred ships of the Danes came to the Frisian islands, beat the Frisians in three fights and took a hundred pounds of silver as tribute.
The emperor Louis gives back to the Frisians who had risen their right to inherit.
On the day after Christmas a great flood goes over Frisia; two thousand four hundred and thirty-seven are counted drowned.
At Meerssen the Ems mouth falls to the East Frankish kingdom. From about now the mound is enlarged northward with clay sods, a street is laid on it, and Emden is a market for its district.
In the autumn the Frisians under Archbishop Rimbert beat the Danes at Norditi, a day's walk to the north. Many of the Danes are drowned by the tide.
history.source: de.wikipedia 'Schlacht bei Norditi', after Adam of Bremen I.41 (?)

history.text: About this year the counts of Werl, a Westphalian house, hold the county of the Ems, and the mound is enlarged again.
Not before this year a timber church is built on a mound of its own to the west, with a graveyard.
A second timber church is built on the place of the first, of oak felled this year.
From about this year until about 1051 pennies are struck here with the names HERIMAN and AMVTHON: the first writing of the name. They are light, three quarters of a gram.
history.source: Giesen, Jaarboek voor Munt- en Penningkunde 95 (2008); Dannenberg 772-773

history.text: In this age, the year not known, a fire burns houses on the mound.
The king orders the county of the Ems handed to Archbishop Adalbert of Hamburg and Bremen. Count Bernhard of Werl does not give it up, and about 1063 the archbishop's man Gottschalk is killed.
history.source: de.wikipedia 'Bernhard II. (Werl)', 'Grafen von Werl', 'Gottschalk von Zutphen'

history.text: Archbishop Adalbert falls from power at the king's court.

eras.text: A summer landing more than a village: a sod rise above the spring tides, plank houses of a few trading households, sheep-houses on the marsh. In 793 the district is in revolt, the chapel up the river is burned and no priest shows his face; in 794 Liudger is back and nobody is punished who comes to be shriven. Bread is dear in 793 and 794.

The first mound with its ditch: forty metres of crowded ground, small houses, looms, a rain pond. Liudger's priests come and go by boat. In 810 the Danes are on the islands and the mound pays its share of the hundred pounds. The flood of Christmas 838 drowns the low marsh and leaves the mound an island for a week.

The mound grows northward, a palisade marks its edge, and a street runs along its crown with narrow houses of traders and craftsmen fronting it. After 870 the Ems mouth is East Frankish and a count's man takes the king's toll (?). The Danes leave the place more or less alone; in 884 they are beaten at Norditi.

A second mound with a farmer's long house and byre, the counts of Werl far away in Westphalia, and from the 940s a timber church on its own mound to the west with the dead laid east and west about it. Emuthon has outgrown Groothusen and Hatzum. The first sea banks are thrown up along the coast about 1000.

A count's market with a mint: light pennies with HERIMAN on one side and AMVTHON on the other go out to the Danes and the east. Plots are ditched and fenced, a fire takes part of the street, and from 1062 the count and the archbishop of Bremen both claim the toll.

sites.name: The creek mouth
sites.see: A muddy creek running into the brown river, boats lying on their bilges on the ebb with a plank laid to the bank. Behind them a strip of empty wet ground and then the mound, low and green, with smoke lying flat over it. Curlews, the suck of mud under feet, and the smell of salt, sheep and peat smoke.
sites.source: Fundchronik Emden 2014 (boats lay in the creek mouth, later the Ratsdelft); Grimm 2010, pp. 14, 18 (empty ground between mound and river; no quay found)

sites.name: The mound
sites.see: A rise of clay sods no wider than a long bowshot is short, ringed by a narrow ditch, with small plank and wattle houses set close. In front, bolts of grey and blue cloth over a rail, cheeses on a board, a ewe tied by one leg; behind, a hundred miles of flat marsh and sky. After the middle of the ninth century a street runs along the crown.
sites.source: Grimm 2010, pp. 12-13, 18-19 (first mound about 40 m, ditch about 800, small houses, the street); before about 800 only a landing is likely (?)

sites.name: The house with the looms
sites.see: A narrow house, three paces wide, with two upright looms against the long wall and the clay weights swinging. A fire on the floor in the middle, a pot of barley and mutton, sleeping benches under hung cloaks. It smells of wet wool, smoke and ale, and somebody is always telling a story at the dark end.
sites.source: Grimm 2010, pp. 12-13 (street houses 2.6 to 3.3 m wide, dwellings and workshops; spindle whorls and cloth scraps); the household is invented

sites.name: The sheep-house on the marsh
sites.see: A long low house of turf with a reed roof on a hump of its own, a mile of salt grass from the mound. Ewes by the hundred, grey-white, a boy with a dog, pools left by the last spring tide. In the summer of 793 somebody is living behind the hurdles at the far end who is not a shepherd.
sites.source: Grimm 2010, chapter 7 (large ewe flocks kept for wool, manure and milk); the hidden priest is the spine's hook (cross_and_grove), invented

sites.name: The burned posts
sites.see: Six black stumps in a square on the west rise, a heap of wet ash, and a cross of two laths that someone has stood up again and someone else has kicked over. From 794 a plank roof stands on new posts beside the old ones, with a wooden board for an altar. Wind, larks, and when a priest has come by boat, a hand bell.
sites.source: invented to carry the spine's burned church (?): the churches of the district were burned in 793 (Altfrid I.22) and Liudger's chapel stood at Leer; no church is attested at Emden itself before the timber church of after 941

sites.name: The rain pond
sites.see: A round pit lined with clay on the side of the mound, holding the only sweet water for a mile. Women with buckets wait their turn and nobody washes in it. On the bank an old woman sits with a knotted cord in her lap, and people who come for water stay to ask her things.
sites.source: Willibald, Life of Boniface 9 (the want of fresh water in almost all Frisia), as cited in peoples/frisian.md; Indiculus superstitionum 10-12 for what Notburg does; the pond itself is not dug up at Emden (?)

sites.name: The sand the tide covers
sites.see: A hard grey sand at the river's edge, bare at the ebb and under a man's height of water at the flood. The free men stand here in a ring when there is law to speak, with the judge on a turf seat and the watch pole behind him, where the men who owe the coast-watch look seaward. Gulls, wind, and voices that carry too far.
sites.source: Lex Frisionum XIV.4 (cases at a public meeting), Additio XI (the shrine-robber led to the sand the tide covers); the coast-watch at river mouths: de.wikipedia 'Geschichte Ostfrieslands'. That the meeting stood on this sand is invented

sites.name: The crossing to the Nesse
sites.see: A flat boat on the mud below the mound and a spit of green across half a mile of fast brown water. A man with a pole waits for the slack. Over there lie Hatzum with its one street, the peat country, and downriver on the far shore Helewyret, where the blind singer lives.
sites.source: de.wikipedia 'Nesserland', 'Hatzum', 'Dollart' (the river ran close under the mound until 1509; there is no Dollart yet); Bernlef of Helewyret: Altfrid I.25

sites.name: The street
sites.see: A trodden way of clay and brushwood along the crown of the mound, a palisade at its end, narrow gables to either side. A man sawing antler into comb plates, a shoemaker with his last between his knees, cat skins pegged on a wall to dry. Hammering, hens, the reek of the tanning tub.
sites.source: Grimm 2010, pp. 13, 18 and chapter 7 (the street; leather, bone, antler and horn work; cat skins); Fundchronik Emden 2001-2003

sites.name: The count's post
sites.see: A post with a horse's skull on it at the head of the creek, a bench, and a man in a Westphalian cloak with a tally stick who counts bales as they come up the plank. He speaks Saxon to his dog and Frisian to everyone else.
sites.source: Grimm 2010, p. 17 (a royal place with toll and mint); the toll is first written of in 1244 and its rate is not known, so its taking from about 870 is a guess (?)

sites.name: The timber church on the west mound
sites.see: A small church of upright oak planks on a mound of its own, apart from the houses, with a reed roof and a bell on a frame beside the door. Graves lie round it with their feet to the east. Inside it is dark and smells of tallow, damp wool and new-cut oak.
sites.source: Grimm 2010, p. 14 (two timber churches, after 941 and 966); kirchengemeindelexikon.de (graves east-west); later the church of Saints Cosmas and Damian, the dedication's date not known (?)

sites.name: The count's die
sites.see: A locked plank house by the toll post. Through the door, when it is open, a block with an iron die set in it, a man with a hammer, and a boy shearing a silver sheet into rounds with a pair of shears. The pennies come out thin, bright and a little crooked.
sites.source: Giesen 2008 (pennies HERIMAN / AMVTHON, about 1020-1051, mean 0.75 g from 88 coins); the mint is known only from its pennies, so the house is invented

people.name: Tetta
people.trait: A widow who makes the cloth, keeps the house where traders sleep, and forgets no face and no debt.
people.want: A dowry in silver for her daughter Folclint, and seed corn enough that the house never begs.
people.fear: A hungry winter, and the count's men asking who slept under her roof in the year of the rising.
people.voice: Dry and quick; counts while she talks and never raises her voice.
people.looks: Forty, lean, strong forearms blue to the elbow from the woad vat, a grey headcloth, a blue gown pinned with a bronze disc, a wooden weaving sword in her hand.
knows: what cloth, wool, cheese and hides fetch here and at Dorestad
who has slept on the mound this year and where they were bound
where the priest is hidden in 793
which households have silver put by

ties.note: her mother's sister, who brought her into the world
her dead husband's brother; she does not ask what he carries at night
she feeds the priest in the sheep-house and has told nobody
he has a seat by her fire whenever he is over the river
the widow at Dorestad buys her blue cloth and sends word of prices
a cousin, the weaver on the old lords' terp; they send each other dye and gossip by the same boats
lodges the island priest when he comes by boat, and tells him who is sick
the bead woman strings her daughters' dowries at her fire in winter

lines.greet: A Dorestad boat. Lay her on the mud by the plank and come up. You eat here, you sleep here, and we talk about cloth in the morning.
lines.greet_again: You again. Your bench is as you left it, and so is what you owe me for the ale.
rumour: They say the count's men lie dead on the Weser. Men who said so loudly at Easter are saying it quietly now.
No bread on this mound since the shearing. A sack of rye buys a bolt of blue and I will not haggle.
A Dane lay here two nights and bought nothing. He looked at the creek at high water and at low. I did not like it.
lines.famine: My girl's dowry is nine ounces in a pot. I would sooner it bought her a husband than barley. Sell me corn at a price I can meet.
lines.known: I told my daughter: that house pays, and comes back. So you are family here, near enough.
lines.saying: A short cloak is a long cloak sold to a Frank.
lines.farewell: Go on the ebb and keep to the west channel. Bring corn.

people.source: invented; the name from the Fulda rent lists (Traditiones Fuldenses); the woman who makes fresum and whose hand is paid a quarter above her rank is Lex Frisionum, Additio III

people.name: Folcger
people.trait: The ferryman of the Nesse crossing, who knows where the channel went last winter and will take a boat in for a penny and a drink.
people.want: To be owed favours by every skipper between the Vlie and the Eider, and to be asked no questions.
people.fear: The coast-watch oath he swore, and the day somebody reminds him of it before the count.
people.voice: Slow, friendly, always looking at the water instead of at you.
people.looks: Thirty-five, broad and short, sun-bleached hair tied back, bare legs grey with mud to the knee, a sounding pole twice his height, a seal-skin cap.
knows: the west channel past Bant, the drying flats and the hour of slack water
which hulls change cargo in the creek after dark, and for whom
what the Danes pay at Ripa and Sliesthorp for a Frankish blade
who is on watch at the river mouth tonight

ties.note: his brother's widow; he mends her roof and she feeds him
he rows the singer over from Helewyret and takes a story for the fare
the Dorestad dealer's casks are shifted here at night into north-bound hulls
the Dane at Sliesthorp who takes what comes out of those casks
the skipper on the inland water who sends quiet cargoes on to him
they trade word of where the channels went after each winter
tells her first when a boat from the north is in the creek
trades news of the sands with the host at Ripa by any boat going either way

lines.greet: You came in by the west channel. Good. The east one is a story people tell. Next time hail me off the Nesse and I will bring you in.
lines.greet_again: The channel moved a rope's length since you were here. I know where. A penny.
rumour: This is the last landing where the king's word runs. After the Weser it is the Saxons, and after them the Danes. So things change boats here.
A man from Dorestad sends wine north. Heavy wine. It clinks. I shift it at night and I have never seen inside a cask.
The watch at the river mouth is two old men and a boy this month. The young ones went east with Unno.
lines.night: If you have anything under the ballast you would rather sell north of the Eider, I know a hull lying in the creek till the moon sets.
lines.pilot: Come out with me three tides and I will show you the flats dry. After that you will not need me, which is bad business, but there it is.
lines.saying: The sea gives every man two chances a day and takes one back.
lines.farewell: Slack water at cock-crow. Miss it and you sit here another tide looking at me.

people.source: invented; no pilot or sea-mark is recorded for the Ems (dossier 1); the law he fears is the coast-watch owed by loyal Frisians and the arms bans of 779, 803 and 805 (the spine's swords_north)

people.name: Liafbraht
people.trait: A young priest of Liudger's chapel up the river, hiding among the ewes with a psalter and a bad cough.
people.want: Passage west to Traiectum before the men who burned his chapel remember he was not in it.
people.fear: Fire, his own people's faces in the light of it, and that he ran too soon.
people.voice: Whispers from habit even in the open; school Latin breaks through when he is frightened.
people.looks: Twenty-five, thin, a week's stubble over the tonsure, a shepherd's grey cloak over a singed dark tunic, a small book wrapped in oiled wool held to his chest.
knows: what happened at the chapel at Leer, and who led it
where Liudger went and by which road he will come back
the names of the households that kept the faith quietly
letters: he can read a tally, a charter or a psalm

ties.note: ordained by him; left behind when he fled
she has fed him for a month at the risk of her house
she knows where he is and has told nobody, which troubles him more than if she had
the bishop at Traiectum, whose school taught him his letters
his master at Saint Martin's, who will pay for news of him (?)
has slept on his floor more than once, coming and going over the Lauwers

lines.greet: Do not say my name out here. You have a boat that goes west? I can pay in prayers now and in silver at Traiectum.
lines.greet_again: You came back. I have counted the ewes four hundred times. Is the boat ready?
rumour: They came at night with Unno's men. I was at a sick bed two miles off. That is the only reason I am telling you this.
The blind man goes from house to house with a bowl of water. He does what I should be doing, and he does not hide.
The old woman at the pond knows I am here. She sent me horehound for the cough. I drank it. God forgive me, it helped.
lines.carried: I will say your name at the altar of Saint Martin every day I live. It is the only coin I have and it does not wear thin.
lines.returned: I am back, by the bishop's order and in your boat. The same people who lit the fire bring me eggs. Nobody speaks of it.
lines.saying: A shepherd who runs is a hireling. I have read it. I ran.

people.source: invented; the priests of the district were driven out about 793 and returned within the year (Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.22); the name from attested Frisian name parts (Liaf-, -braht)

people.name: Notburg
people.trait: The wise woman of the Ems mouth: herbs, births, knots against fever, the right words at a spring; baptised twice by order and unmoved both times.
people.want: The old customs left alone at the edges: the silence at the spring, a feast at the graves in the dark of the year.
people.fear: Not the priests, who only talk: the count's men, and being forgotten.
people.voice: Kind, exact, a little mocking; calls Liudger 'the Utrecht boy'.
people.looks: Past sixty, small, straight-backed, grey plaits under a dark cloth, a pouch of dried herbs, a knotted cord and a small knife at her girdle, a staff of ash.
knows: herbs, births and fevers, and what a cough means
what the weather will do by the smell of the mud
what was done to shrine-robbers on the tide sand in her mother's day
every child born on this shore for forty years, and whose it really is

ties.note: they are of an age and know the same stories
he breaks what she tends, and asks after her health
her sister's daughter
she doses the hidden priest and enjoys his shame at it
she knew his mother on the islands and asks after his knee
sent a fever cord west by a boatman, to an ale-wife she has never seen
sent her a salve by a skipper and the making of it by word of mouth; has never seen her
a kinsman of her mother's on the old lords' terp, by his own reckoning (?)
people who cannot reach the priest for a fever cross the Lauwers to her; he knows it
brings people over the Lauwers to her for fevers, and says nothing to the priest
bores the amber she hangs on children against the fever, and asks nothing
the same person
an old woman far to the east whom she will never meet: a Frisian skipper carried a bundle of dried root from one to the other, and a different root back
a woman who casts lots on an island of the Svear: a skipper told each of the other, and each sends a greeting by any boat going that way

lines.greet: Sit. You have salt in a cut on that hand and you are favouring your left side. Show me the hand. The side we will come to.
lines.greet_again: The Dorestad one. The hand healed. I knew it would; I tied the knot myself.
rumour: The churches burned and the priests ran. People say the old gods have come home. I say they never left; they only stopped talking.
The Utrecht boy will be back before the geese. He always comes back. He is polite about it, which is the worst of him.
A north wind with a spring tide at the dark of the moon. Drive your beasts up before it, not during.
lines.omen: You want to know if the voyage goes well. Is the boat sound? Are the men fed? Then it goes well. That will be a cheese.
lines.priest: I know who is in Tetta's sheep-house. I have known for a month. If I wanted him found he would be found.
lines.saying: Twice they put me in the water. I came out wet both times, and that was all.
lines.farewell: Draw your water in silence and you will not need me. Nobody does, so I will see you again.

people.source: invented (the spine's cast.notburg); what she does is the list of the Indiculus superstitionum (10 amulets and knots, 11 springs, 12 incantations) and Fosite's silent spring (Altfrid I.22)

people.name: Bernlef
people.trait: Loved by his neighbours because he is courteous and knows the deeds of the men of old and the wars of kings by heart; kept the secret of his healing as he was told.
people.want: To keep both: the old kings' stories, and the psalms Liudger is teaching him.
people.voice: Easy and courteous; begins every answer with a story about a king.
people.looks: About sixty, big-framed and gentle, white hair to the shoulder, eyes that look a little past you from habit, a blue-grey cloak, a stick he no longer needs; his wife leads him by the sleeve out of long use.
knows: the deeds of the old kings of the Frisians and their wars, from Finn son of Folcwald down
every household between the Ems and the Lauwers and who is sick in it
psalms, as many as Liudger has taught him
riddles, and who on this coast can answer them

ties.note: who healed him
they know the same stories
the island priest asks him for the old names of things
the ferryman rows him over for the price of a story
the Northman has riddles of his own and they trade them like blows
an old man west of the Lauwers who knows the same stories of the old kings
has a seat by her fire whenever he is over the river
the same person

lines.greet: There was a king, Finn, Folcwald's son, who had guests over winter and it ended badly. You are a guest. Sit, and we will see that it ends well.
lines.greet_again: I know that step on the plank. Three years blind teaches the ears. Welcome back, merchant.
rumour: A child at the far sheep-house will not see morning. No priest dares the road, so I go, with a bowl of water. Row me over.
Liudger told me: when a child is dying, the water and the words, and God sees to the rest. Eighteen now. Two of them lived.
Old Radbod stood with one foot in the font, they say, and stepped back out. I sing it. I do not say it is true.
lines.healing: He bade me tell no one how my sight came back, while he lived. So ask me about kings instead.
lines.psalm: I am learning the psalms. They are also about kings, and wars, and one man in trouble. I find I knew them already.
lines.saying: A story is the only cargo that weighs nothing and pays at every landing.
lines.farewell: Go well. When you come again I will have the next part, if the dark has not.

people.source: Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.25-26 (ed. Diekamp 1881): blind three years, healed by Liudger, sang the deeds of the men of old and the wars of kings, baptised eighteen dying infants in the rising, learned the psalms. He lived at Helewyret (Holwierde) across the Ems mouth and is not recorded at Emden; his birth year is a guess and his death year is not known (?). Finn Folcwalding: Widsith and Beowulf

people.name: Liudger
people.trait: A Frisian nobleman's son taught at Utrecht and York: gentle with people, hard on shrines, always carrying books.
people.want: Priests, books and a bell for the Frisians and the western Saxons; a house of monks on his own land at Werden.
people.fear: The Northmen: he dreamed of the sun fleeing over the sea from the north with black cloud behind it, and wept.
people.voice: Plain Frisian with a little of York's English in it; asks before he tells.
people.looks: About fifty, tall and spare, tonsured, a travel-stained cloak over a priest's tunic, a book satchel, a small cross of bronze; he rides a horse and leads it through villages.
knows: who rose in 793 and who only watched, and that he means to punish neither
York, its school and its books, and his master Alcuin's letters
the road up the Ems into Westphalia and who holds each ford
what a book costs, in calves and in a scribe's years

ties.note: his master at York
gave him back his sight and taught him the psalms
baptised him on Fosite's island and made him a priest
breaks what she tends
ordained him for the chapel at Leer
Utrecht's bishop is his old school's lord
taught him his letters at Utrecht; remembers a slow reader with a good heart
they shared a bench under Gregory; he went to York, and Radger kept the school
does not remember him among the boys at Utrecht, and is too kind to say so (?)
taught him his letters at Utrecht, and left him a psalter leaf in his own hand
knew his father's hall east of the IJssel, and asks after the family
the boy who carried planks when he rebuilt Lebuin's church, and is now its priest
the ferryman has carried him and his horse many times, and asked his faith once
one of the Utrecht boys who heard him talk of the terps, and went to live among them
the old herdsman who watched the shrine's silver carried down to the boat; Liudger spoke kindly to him and has not forgotten his face
was on the same ship home from York when Aldger was the ship's boy; baptised his sisters
buried her husband and baptised her daughters
his pupil at Doccinga from 777 until the priests were driven out
heard her story of the martyr's day for seven years, and wrote none of it down
a priest at Cologne who thinks him the only man who preaches to Saxons as if they could hear
his Saxon and Frisian districts answer to Cologne; Hildebold is said to have consecrated him bishop in 805 (?)
taught the hostage the Creed in her own tongue and did not ask her to mean it yet
the same person, at his house on the Ruhr from 799
the steward at the Ruhr mouth sold him nothing and helped him with everything; a Mass is owed for the man's wife
the ferryman carries his books up the Ruhr for a psalm a trip
a small boy at York who carried his ink, and wept when the Frisians left
shared his bread at York with a small boy who is now a scribe at Jarrow
both men of Alcuin's school; his Saxons and the bishop's hostages are the same war
the same person

lines.greet: You are the Dorestad merchant. Did you come by Traiectum? Is the school full? And tell me, were you here last summer, when I was not?
lines.greet_again: Good. Sit a moment. What are they saying at Dorestad about the Northmen? I ask everyone. Nobody tells me what I hope to hear.
rumour: Whoever comes to be shriven goes home shriven. I have told the count's men I keep no list. It is true. I burned it.
I want a bell for this shore. A bell is heard where a priest is not. Do you know what bronze costs at Colonia this year?
I dreamed the sun fled over the sea from the north, and cloud after it. My sister asked why I wept. I could not make it sound like nothing.
lines.carried: You carried Liafbraht out when it was dangerous to know him. I do not forget, and neither does Saint Martin's.
lines.bishop: They have made me a bishop, at Mimigernaford among the Saxons. I asked to stay a priest. I was told that was pride as well.
lines.saying: Break the shrine and spare the man. He will need somewhere to stand afterwards.
lines.farewell: God keep the boat. If you pass York, there is a book I lent in the year of the comet.

people.source: Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri, book I (ed. Diekamp 1881); de.wikipedia 'Liudger' for 787, 805 and 26 March 809. He had charge of Emisga from 787 and was driven out about 793, but no source places him at Emden itself: the game does (?). The 'year of the comet' is our flourish (?)

people.name: Landric
people.trait: Island-born: knows the old rites from the inside and preaches against them without scorn.
people.want: A church that stays standing on Fosite's island; his father's people left alone by both kings.
people.fear: Danish ships at the island; being called a traitor to his father's gods by people he baptised.
people.voice: Slow and careful; uses sea words for holy things.
people.looks: Thirty, weathered like a fisherman under the tonsure, a priest's dark tunic, a seal-skin cloak against the rain, a small wooden box with the oil and the host.
knows: Fosite's island: the landing, the spring, the cattle no one may touch
which Danish ships have been seen off the islands this year
the old words for things, which he asks Bernlef to confirm
how each household's share of the tribute was reckoned in 810

ties.note: who lifted him from the font
asks him the old names
she lodges him when he comes by boat and tells him who is sick
island people both; their mothers were of one house (?)
the priest at Boniface's church, with whom he shares a boat at Easter
she wove the cloth for his Mass stone; he has promised to marry her daughter properly, before the cross
asks him the old names of things, and does not scold him for knowing them
the same person

lines.greet: You came in on the flood. So did I, thirty years ago, in my father's boat, to be baptised. Different cargo. Sit down.
lines.greet_again: Still afloat, both of us. That is most of what I pray for, if I am honest.
rumour: On my father's island men drew water in silence, for fear. Now they draw it in silence from habit. I count that as half the work done.
Two hundred sails off the islands. The Danish king wants a hundred pounds. Each mound is told its share, and ours is nine pounds.
They drove the cattle inland to the peat. A cow walks slower than a ship sails. We lost three fights; I buried men from all of them.
lines.share: Pay your part with the mound and the Danes will let your sail be this season. I do not call it right. I call it the tide.
lines.saying: The Church is a boat. Nobody aboard likes everybody aboard, and nobody gets out.
lines.farewell: Fair wind. If you see the island, look for a roof with a cross. Tell me if it still stands.

people.source: Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.22: son of a chief of Fosetesland, baptised by Liudger, ordained and 'for many years set over the teaching of the Frisians'. Only that is recorded; his years, his presence here and the mound's share of nine pounds are ours (?)

people.name: Imma
people.trait: The moneyer's wife, who keeps the house with the looms on the street and says it has been in the women of her line since before the mound had a ditch.
people.want: The count's die kept on this mound and not moved over the river to the archbishop's new markets.
people.fear: Fire in the street, and her husband being asked whose pennies are light.
people.voice: Brisk and amused; names your forefathers before she names her price.
people.looks: Thirty, round-faced, a white linen headcloth, a dark blue gown with a silver penny on a cord at the neck, shears on her girdle, ink-black fingertips from the dye.
knows: what an Emuthon penny weighs against one of Tiel or Daventre, and who will take which
which Danes and Svear buy the light pennies by the bag
the count's quarrel with the archbishop of Bremen over the toll
an old house story: a Dorestad merchant who sold corn to the mound in a hungry year

ties.note: eight mothers back, by the house's own reckoning
the heavy-penny men up the IJssel call her husband's coin a short cloak (?)
the moneyer at Doccinga, who strikes the same light Frisian weight and trades dies' gossip with her husband

lines.greet: A house from the Rhine mouth? My mother's mothers kept a bench for one. Sit on it. It has been mended since.
lines.greet_again: Back with heavy pennies, I hope. My husband will give you five of ours for four of those, and smile.
rumour: Our pennies say Heriman and Amuthon. They are light, yes. They are also here, which the Tiel ones are not.
The archbishop has a mint and a toll over the river now, at Winsum. He wants ours too. The count says come and take it.
The Danes like our pennies. They weigh them anyway. A Dane would weigh his mother.
lines.fire: Four houses went in one night. We passed the dies out through the wall before we passed the children. I am not proud of the order.
lines.known: They say your house sold corn here at a fair price in a famine, before there was a church. We keep cloth back for you. It is owed.
lines.saying: A light penny buys as much bread as a heavy one, if you are quick.
lines.farewell: Go carefully past Bant. There is less of it every year.

people.source: invented; the pennies are Giesen 2008 and Dannenberg 772-773; Winsum and Garrelsweer granted to Archbishop Adalbert 1047-1057 (Giesen 2008); the undated fire is Grimm 2010 p. 19; the name is in the Fulda rent lists

people.name: Gerlint
people.trait: Strings beads and bores amber on a board at the foot of the mound: patient, sharp-eyed, and the only person at Emuthon who is glad of a Danish boat.
people.want: Raw amber by the sack from the north, and yellow glass from the Rhine that stays yellow.
people.fear: Her eyes going before her fingers do.
people.voice: Soft, and never looks up from the bead; names the price to the bead.
people.looks: A small woman of about thirty with a squint from close work, a blue headcloth, strings of amber and glass round her neck as her whole shop, a bow drill in her lap.
knows: what amber costs raw at Ripa and bored here
which strings are in fashion on the terps this year and which at Dorestad
every Danish boat that has lain in the creek, and what its master wanted
who has a daughter to marry, by what her mother buys

ties.note: her cousin the bead man of Westergo, who walks the terps; she buys his amber rough and sends him glass
sits at Tetta's fire in winter and strings beads for the daughters' dowries
bores the amber the wise woman hangs on children against the fever, and asks no questions about it
the ferryman tells her first when a boat from the north is in the creek

lines.greet: Mind the board. Amber on the left, glass on the right, and the string in the middle is spoken for.
lines.greet_again: The boat with the careful master. Did the yellow ones sell at Dorestad? I said they would.
rumour: A Dane paid me in a cut coin with writing like worms. My cousin had one the same. I bored a hole in mine; it hangs well.
Amber is dear this year. The Danes are keeping it for a market of their own, they say, with a wall round it.
Tetta's daughter will have nine ounces with her when she marries. I know, because I am stringing the tenth.
lines.saying: A bead is a hole with something round it. So is a bargain.
lines.farewell: Bring me yellow glass from the Rhine. Real yellow. I will know.

people.source: invented, to make real the cousin on the Ems of wijnaldum.gerbrand. Amber and glass beads are common in the Frisian terps and at Emden (Stilke 1995 (?)); a bead seller is not recorded there.

stories.title: The priest in the sheep-house
stories.summary: In the summer of the rising a young priest is hiding among Tetta's ewes and wants passage west to Traiectum. Whoever carries him is known afterwards to Liudger, to the bishop's house, and to the people on the mound who watched the boat go.
stories.picture: A turf sheep-house at dusk on the open marsh; a thin man in a shepherd's cloak, a wrapped book against his chest, looking out between hurdles at a boat on the mud far off.

beats.text: Tetta sets out one bowl more than there are people at the fire, and carries it out herself after dark. Ask, and she looks at you for a long time before she answers.
Liafbraht asks for passage to Traiectum. He can pay nothing now. Taking him aboard sets ms_carried_priest; the risen men search boats at the river mouth while Unno's word still runs.
Notburg says she has known for a month, and that the old gods have come home and have no need of one frightened boy. She will neither help nor hinder.
At Saint Martin's the bishop's house takes the priest in and remembers the boat. In 794 a priest is sent back to Emuthon and needs a hull: the same hull, if it will go.
Liudger is back. A plank roof goes up beside the burned posts, and nobody is punished who comes to be shriven. He asks who carried his priest, and thanks them in front of the mound.

endings.how: The priest was taken west and, in 794, brought back.
endings.text: Liafbraht serves the shore for seven years more and says the merchant's name at the altar. Liudger counts the house among his friends.
endings.reward: Liudger and the bishop's house at Traiectum hold the merchant dear (npc priest feeling up; deed carried_letters); alms and Mass here cost nothing; a letter of thanks that eases the toll at Traiectum for a season.

endings.how: The merchant would not take the risk and sailed without him.
endings.text: The priest walks west along the coast by night and reaches Doccinga half dead. He bears no grudge. Tetta says nothing, and charges for the ale.
endings.reward: Nothing lost but Tetta's warmth for a year; the story can still be mended by carrying the returning priest from Traiectum in 794.

endings.how: The merchant told the risen men where he was.
endings.text: They put him on a horse and drive him over the district's edge with his book burned. Nobody on the mound forgets who spoke; when Liudger comes back he prays for the merchant by name, which is worse.
endings.reward: A purse of 60 d from Unno's men and safe passage that summer; Tetta's house is shut to the merchant, and the bishop's men at Traiectum search his boat for years.

stories.reward: A friend in Liudger, standing with the church from Traiectum to the Ems, and a house on the mound that trusts you with what it hides.

stories.title: The bowl of water
stories.summary: While no priest dares the road, the singer Bernlef goes from house to house baptising children who will not live till morning, as Liudger told him. He needs someone to row him over the Ems and along the creeks, and pays in the old kings' stories.
stories.picture: A big white-haired man stepping out of a small boat onto a mud bank at night, a wooden bowl held level in both hands, his wife at his sleeve, one lit doorway on a low mound ahead.

beats.text: Bernlef and his wife wait for the ferry with a bowl and a skin of sweet water. The ferryman is drunk. Will the merchant's boat take him over to the sheep-houses and back, tide by tide?
By Tetta's fire he tells Finn Folcwalding and the winter guests, a part each night, and stops where the tale is best. He has baptised eighteen; two lived.
At Boniface's church they have heard of the blind man who can see and want to know if it is true. What the merchant says there comes back to Bernlef by the next boat.
Bernlef dies old and full of days, and his wife fifteen days after him. The mound asks the merchant, who rowed him, to say what he was told.

endings.how: The merchant rowed him to every house and kept the secret of his healing.
endings.text: Bernlef gives the house the whole of Finn's tale and a riddle no one on the coast has answered. At his grave the merchant is asked to speak, and is believed.
endings.reward: sets ms_bernlef_met; the old poem Deor for the chest (give_text deor); a riddle; the crew's heart up whenever she lies here; every household on the Ems mouth knows the boat.

endings.how: The merchant heard the stories by the fire but would not lose tides rowing.
endings.text: Folcger sobers up and rows him. Bernlef is as courteous as before and tells the short versions.
endings.reward: sets ms_bernlef_met; one tale and a rumour that is true; no more.

endings.how: The merchant told at Doccinga how the blind man was healed, while Liudger lived.
endings.text: Pilgrims come over the Ems to stare at Bernlef, and Liudger asks him, gently, who talked. Bernlef says a king's story instead of answering.
endings.reward: 20 d from the curious at Doccinga; Bernlef still greets the merchant but tells no more tales; Liudger's regard falls.

stories.reward: A text for the chest, a riddle, and the name of a man who rowed the singer: worth a welcome on every mound between the Ems and the Lauwers.

stories.title: Bread for cloth
stories.summary: The mound grows sheep, not corn, and buys its bread every year. In the hungry years, 793 and 794 and again from 805, it will pay for grain in cloth, cheese, hides, or the silver put by for a daughter's dowry, and it remembers for generations what it was charged.
stories.picture: A narrow house with looms: a lean woman tipping a small pot of hack-silver onto a cloth beside an open sack of rye, a girl of fifteen watching from the bench.

beats.text: No bread on the mound. A sack of rye or barley fetches a bolt of blue cloth, or two cheeses and a hide; nobody haggles. The king's price of 794 is known here only by hearsay.

Tetta offers the nine ounces of her daughter's dowry for corn to last till harvest. The merchant can take the silver, take cloth at her price instead, or sell at the king's price and wait to be paid at the shearing.
At Dorestad Thiadbod holds grain and waits; Thiadburg sells hers at the king's price. Either will load a boat for the Ems, and each asks what the mound is paying.
Two hundred years on, the woman of the house with the looms knows the story and keeps cloth back for the heirs of the house that sold corn fairly.

beats.when: (year = 805 and month >= 10) or year = 806 or (year = 807 and month <= 8)
beats.text: In the second hungry time a north-bound hull lies in the creek and pays silver by weight for rye, over any Frankish price. The emperor's law of that year forbids selling food out of the realm, and the mound watches which way the sacks go. (Selling over the side sets hy_ran_grain.)

endings.how: Grain was sold at or under the king's price, or on trust until the shearing.
endings.text: Folclint keeps her dowry and marries on the mound. Tetta's house holds the merchant's goods without rent and sells him cloth before anyone else sees it.
endings.reward: sets hy_fed_poor; a factor on the mound (flag unlock_factor_emuthon); first choice of the new cloth each Easter at the weaver's own price; deed fair_dealing.

endings.how: The merchant took the dowry silver, or cloth at a famine price.
endings.text: Nine ounces of silver for a boatload of rye is the best trade of the year. Folclint goes to a husband across the river with a cow instead. Tetta still sells to the merchant, at the price she gives strangers.
endings.reward: about 180 d in hack-silver or its worth in cloth; sets hy_sold_dear; the bed at Tetta's is paid for from now on, and Imma's house in 1020 has heard a different story.

endings.how: The merchant gave part of the cargo at the church door, or what served for one.
endings.text: Bernlef makes four lines about it that are still said on the mound when the merchant's grandson comes in.
endings.reward: sets hy_fed_poor; deed gave_alms; standing in the region up; no silver.

stories.reward: A house that keeps your goods and your bed, and a name on this shore that outlasts you.

stories.title: The mound's share
stories.summary: In 810 two hundred Danish ships lie at the Frisian islands and King Godfred asks a hundred pounds of silver. Each mound is told its share; cattle are driven inland; three fights are lost.
stories.picture: The mound at dawn seen from the creek: people passing a wooden chest hand to hand down to the mud, a line of cattle being driven away along the horizon, and far out, masts.

beats.text: At Ripa the king's men gather ships and a Frisian hull is asked whose side she is on. A merchant who listens can carry warning home (sets gf_warned).
Because word came in time, the mound's silver is in the peat and its cattle are over the river before the sails show. The share is still asked, but there is less to take.
The free men stand in the ring. The mound's share is told off household by household, and a stranger with a boat and silver aboard is asked for his part like anyone else (sets gf_paid_share).
Folcger wants every hull that floats to carry ewes and children up the Ems on the flood. It pays nothing and it takes three tides.
Landric buries men from three lost fights. By autumn Godfred is dead, killed by one of his own, and the fleet has gone home. The silver has not come back.
At Dorestad every boat is counted for the emperor's host, and word of the two hundred sails is three days old when it is cried on the dams.

endings.how: The merchant paid his part with the mound.
endings.text: The Danish ships let his sail be that season, and the mound counts him one of its own from then on.
endings.reward: costs about 60 d; sets gf_paid_share; the fleet's cards pass him by in 810; a plot offered on the mound when it is next enlarged (flag unlock_plot_emuthon).

endings.how: The merchant brought warning from Ripa before the fleet came.
endings.text: The mound loses less than any other on the coast. Landric tells it at Doccinga and at Wijnaldum; skippers the merchant has never met buy him ale for years.
endings.reward: sets gf_warned; standing in the region up sharply; Folcger teaches him the flats for nothing (flag unlock_pilot_ems); a gift of twelve bolts of cloth.

endings.how: The merchant slipped out on the night ebb with his silver aboard.
endings.text: He keeps his silver. The share he did not pay is paid by Tetta's household among others, and they know it.
endings.reward: nothing lost; the mound's feeling falls; next visit the toll is asked twice over and the bench at Tetta's is taken.

stories.reward: A place among the mound's own people: a plot, or the pilot's knowledge of the Ems, according to what was done.

stories.title: Heriman's light pennies
stories.summary: From about 1020 the count's die at Emuthon strikes pennies of three quarters of a gram, where Tiel and Daventre strike a full gram and more. The same face value in lighter silver: a house that knows where each penny is counted and where it is weighed can live on the difference.
stories.picture: A hand holding a small folding balance: one fat penny in one pan, one thin bright penny in the other, the beam tipped; behind it a boy shearing rounds from a silver sheet.

beats.text: The moneyer gives five of his pennies for four of Tiel's and thinks he has the better of it. Imma says who takes the light coin by count: shepherds, the count's toll, small markets along the coast.
At Daventre the heavy-penny men will not take AMVTHON coin except by weight, and say so with pleasure. They sell good pennies for cloth.
The Danes weigh everything and care nothing for the name on it. A bag of Emuthon pennies is silver to them, no worse and no better.

The archbishop of Bremen has a mint and a toll over the river and wants this one. The count's man asks every skipper which lord's pennies he would rather be paid in, and writes the answers on a stick.

At the bishop's mint a merchant of the Stathe holds out a handful of AMVTHON pennies he was paid by count, and the moneyer sets his little scale level. Whoever passed them makes the weight good, or clears himself by his oath.

endings.how: The merchant dealt openly: light coin where it is counted, heavy where it is weighed, and said which was which.
endings.text: The moneyer makes him a witness to the die, and the count's man lets his bales through on a nod.
endings.reward: a steady gain of a fifth on silver carried between the Ems and the IJssel; toll eased here; the house is asked to witness the die (deed fair_dealing).

endings.how: The merchant passed Emuthon pennies by count where full weight was expected.
endings.text: It works twice. The third time a reeve has a balance on the table, and the name of the house goes round the IJssel towns before the boat does.
endings.reward: up to 300 d quickly; then goods held for judgement at Daventre or Tiel (deed goods_seized) and a rival who will not forget.

endings.how: The merchant told the count's man he would be paid in the count's pennies, and stood by it when the archbishop's man asked.
endings.text: When Gottschalk is killed about 1063 and the county stays with Werl, the house is remembered as one that did not change sides in the creek.
endings.reward: a charter of toll freedom on the Ems mouth from the count (flag unlock_charter_emuthon) (?); the archbishop's markets at Winsum are cold to the house.

stories.reward: The knowledge of two weights of penny, worth a fifth on every bag, and in the end a count's or an archbishop's favour, not both.

stories.title: The year of the rising
stories.summary: In 793 the East Frisians have risen with the Saxons under Unno and Eilrat: the churches east of the Lauwers are burned, the priests driven out, and the count's men lie dead on the Weser. A boat from a Frankish port lands in the middle of it, and a year later, when the priests and the king's peace come back, everyone on the mound remembers what its master said and to whom.
stories.picture: The grey sand ring at low water: armed free men standing in a circle round two speakers, a small trading boat on the mud behind them with its master watching from the bow, smoke of a burned church on the far skyline.

beats.text: The free men stand in the ring on the sand the tide covers. Unno's word runs here this summer: no tithe, no count, no priests. A Dorestad boat is asked whose man her master is, and the ring waits for the answer.

Boats are searched at the river mouth for Franks and for books. A priest is hiding among Tetta's ewes, and she has told nobody but the one who counted her bowls. (Carrying him sets ms_carried_priest.)
No priest dares the road, so the blind man who was given his sight goes from house to house with a bowl of water, baptising children who will not live till morning. (Rowing him sets ms_bernlef_met.)
On the IJssel the host's buyers want to hear from anyone who has been on the Ems: how many are out, and whether they have boats. What is said there is carried east with the oats.
Hartwin the steward asks, tally in hand, which Frisian landings paid the king's dues this year and which did not. He writes nothing down while you are in the room.
The priests come back, and Liudger with them. Nobody is punished who comes to be shriven. Tetta still wonders who will ask her whose shoes stood by her door in the year of the rising.

endings.how: You traded on the mound through the rising and told the steward and the host's buyers nothing they could use.
endings.text: When the king's peace comes back nobody on the mound is named, and nobody forgets why. Tetta keeps your goods as she keeps her own, and her daughters after her.
endings.reward: Tetta's house as a factor (flag unlock_factor_emuthon); fast friends on the mound; the steward at Dorestad a little cooler.

endings.how: You took the hidden priest west under your sailcloth, and brought a priest back when it was over.
endings.text: Liudger thanks you in front of the mound, which is worth more there than a count's seal. The men who searched boats in 793 buy your grain in 794 and do not meet your eye.
endings.reward: The spine's flag ms_carried_priest; Liudger's word to the bishop (surety on the count's day); your house's name said at the new church.

endings.how: You told the count's steward which landings had turned the king's men away.
endings.text: The count's men come to the Ems with a list. Fines are taken in cattle, and one house on the mound is burned. Your toll at Dorestad is light for a year, and no one at Emuthon will lodge you for a generation.
endings.reward: Toll eased at Dorestad; the steward's trust; shunned at Emuthon, and the story follows the boat along the terps.

stories.reward: A house at the Ems mouth that trusts you through every later trouble, or the king's officers' good opinion and a coast that remembers.

stories.title: The hull in the creek
stories.summary: Emuthon is the last landing where the Frankish king's word runs, so it is where things change boats. Twelve bundles that left the Rhine as wine come up the Almere by night and lie in the creek until the moon is down; the ferryman of the Nesse sees them into a north-bound hull, and has never once looked inside.
stories.picture: A creek mouth in the last of the moonlight: a small boat riding deep beside a dark clinker hull with no lantern, a short broad man with a sounding pole standing between them on the mud, counting on his fingers.

beats.text: Thiadbod, friendly as ever, asks whether you would lie one night at the eel stakes below Medemelacha. He says the toll is seen to. He does not say for what.
Eilbern brings his boat alongside without a light: twelve bundles an arm long, for a man called Folcger at the Ems mouth. Take them, leave them, or go to the toll man at first light.

Folcger counts your waterline with his eyes. At moonset the bundles go over the side into a hull bound north, and he names the buyer: Asulf at Sliesthorp, who pays for blades in silver or in people. (Sets sw_ran_blades and sw_buyer_known.)
The count's man reads the emperor's law in the ring: no arms and no mail to the east or north, the goods forfeit, half to the man who finds them. Folcger stands in the ring with the rest and nods.
At the Danes' market a dealer in people has a Frankish blade on his hip with a cask stain in the fuller. He knows the Ems ferryman's name, and now he knows yours.

endings.how: You carried the bundles to the creek and handed them over at moonset.
endings.text: A hundred and fifty pennies by weight, and Folcger's trust: there is always a hull in the creek for you after that. Meinburg at Medemelacha sets your ale down hard, and the toll men of the coast begin to look at your waterline.
endings.reward: 150 d; the unlock emuthon.night_hull; the spine's flags sw_ran_blades and sw_buyer_known; a blade that may one day come back up the river in a raider's hand.

endings.how: You sank the bundles in the creek and said the toll man had taken them.
endings.text: Folcger does not believe you and cannot say so. Thiadbod is as friendly as ever, and never offers you an errand again. The bundles are still there, under two fathoms of Ems mud.
endings.reward: Nothing in silver; a clear name with the king's men; Thiadbod's long memory.

endings.how: You took the bundles to the watch at the river mouth, or told the toll man at Medemelacha before you ever loaded them.
endings.text: The blades are forfeit and half their worth is the finder's by the emperor's law, when the count's steward gets round to paying it. Eilbern is not hanged, because nobody saw his face. He knows who did.
endings.reward: Toll eased on the Frisian coast; the toll man's nod at Medemelacha; a feud with Thiadbod's house and no friends on the night water.

stories.reward: Good silver and a place in the quiet trade north, or the toll men's trust and a rival who smiles at you for the rest of his life.

works.name: A brushwood way over the mud
works.what: Bundles of willow and alder laid on stakes from the creek to the foot of the mound, so that bales go up dry and a boat is loaded in one ebb. It has to be relaid after every hard winter.
works.needs: Brushwood and stakes brought down the Ems, for the marsh has no trees; the mound's leave, which Tetta or Folcger can get you.
works.gives: Loading and unloading here takes half the time; porters cost less; the mound's feeling rises because everyone uses it.
works.picture: A track of bound brushwood across shining mud from a beached boat to a green mound, two men carrying a bale on a pole along it.
works.source: invented in the period's manner: no quay has been found and empty ground lay between mound and river (Grimm 2010 p. 18); brushwood trackways are common on the marsh coast (?)

works.name: A bell for the shore
works.what: A small bell of sheet iron, riveted and brazed with bronze in the manner of the Irish and English hand bells, hung on a frame by the burned posts. Liudger wants it more than he wants a roof.
works.needs: Liudger or Landric living; iron and bronze, or the bell itself bought at Colonia or Eoforwic and carried here.
works.gives: Liudger's and Landric's regard; Mass is said here whenever she lies in on a feast; in fog the bell is rung for a boat that is expected, which makes the way in surer.
works.picture: A square-shouldered iron hand bell on a timber frame beside six burned posts, a tall thin priest reaching up to it, marsh and sky behind.
works.source: Liudger's want of bells is the spine's (cast.liudger); riveted iron hand bells are the kind of the eighth and ninth centuries (?); no bell is recorded at Emden

works.name: A watch pole and fire on the Nesse
works.what: A tall pole with a basket for a fire on the spit across the river, and a hut for the men who owe the coast-watch. From it sails can be seen an hour sooner than from the mound.
works.needs: The free men's agreement at the tide sand; a load of oak for the pole.
works.gives: Warning of fleets reaches the mound in time to drive the beasts up: in 810 it counts as warning brought (as gf_warned). Folcger can no longer shift cargo at night unseen, and says so.
works.picture: A lone pole with an iron fire basket on a grass spit, a turf hut at its foot, a boy looking down the estuary toward a line of small sails.
works.source: the coast-watch at the river mouths owed by loyal Frisians (de.wikipedia 'Geschichte Ostfrieslands'); the pole and fire are invented in the period's manner

works.name: A share in raising the mound
works.what: The mound is widened northward with cut clay sods, a season's work for every household and hired diggers besides. Whoever pays for a stretch has the right to a narrow plot fronting the new street.
works.needs: A friend on the mound to speak for a stranger; silver for diggers through one summer.
works.gives: A house plot on the street (as unlock_plot_emuthon): goods kept dry through the winter floods, a bed of your own, and a voice at the tide sand.
works.picture: Men with wooden spades stacking square clay sods against the side of a mound, a new palisade behind them, a woman pacing out a narrow plot with a cord.
works.source: Grimm 2010, p. 18: the first mound enlarged northward with clay sods in the mid ninth to early tenth century, with a street and a palisade

works.name: Oak for the church on the west mound
works.what: The first timber church is small and already leaning. A new one needs oak, and oak does not grow on the marsh: it must be bought in Westphalia and floated down the Ems.
works.needs: Oak timber carried down the Ems, three boatloads; the bishop of Mimigernaford's leave, which the priest here asks for.
works.gives: A grave for the house by the church wall and a Mass each year on the giver's day; standing with the church across the bishopric; sanctuary here is never refused you.
works.picture: Carpenters raising upright oak planks into a sill beam on a small mound, an older smaller church beside it half taken down, graves around.
works.source: Grimm 2010, p. 14: the second timber church is tree-ring dated to 966, under Bishop Hildebold (941-969); that a merchant paid for it is invented

ships.note: Flat-bottomed boats for the creeks and the ferry, patched many times; sold when a fisherman dies or a ferryman drinks.
ships.picture: A tarred flat-bottomed boat lying on its side on the mud, a man scraping weed off her bottom.
ships.source: invented from the place: fishers, fowlers and a crossing are certain (Grimm 2010, ch. 7); no ship find at Emden

ships.note: River freighters on a log keel come down the Ems from the oak country of Westphalia with timber and grain, and their owners sometimes sell the boat with the cargo and walk home.
ships.picture: A long dark hollowed-oak boat with one raised plank a side, stacked with timber, nosing into the creek mouth.
ships.source: the Ems road into Westphalia (Grimm 2010, p. 17); the boat type as at Utrecht (ships.md); that such hulls were sold here is a guess (?)

ships.note: The priests of the Ems mouth are served by boat from Liudger's houses, and after 805 from the bishop's; between feasts their coaster can be hired with her steersman.
ships.picture: A small beamy sailing boat with a cross chalked on her stem, drawn up below the burned posts.
ships.source: invented from Liudger's mission by water (Altfrid I.22: he sailed to Fosite's island); (?)

ships.note: Once Emuthon is a market for its district, sea-going traders of the Frisian kind lie in the creek and now and then change hands here; nothing so large is built on a shore without timber.
ships.picture: A round-hulled trader with one mast, high at stem and stern, sitting upright on the mud at low water with the mound behind.
ships.source: Grimm 2010, p. 17 (Emden established as a regional market after 870; coastwise run between the Rhine mouth and Hedeby); the timberless coast: Design/research_trade_seasons_and_hints.md 2.2

sayings.text: 'What is the good of those little napkins? I cannot cover myself with them in bed.' On the mound this is told as a joke against the king, who paid the long price all the same.
sayings.source: Notker, Deeds of Charles I.34 (tr. A. J. Grant 1907): Charlemagne on the short cloaks the Frisians sold

sayings.text: Dear is the welcome guest to the Frisian wife, when the vessel stands: she calls him in, washes his weedy garment, and gives him new raiment.
sayings.source: Exeter Book, Gnomic Verses (tr. B. Thorpe 1842), as quoted in peoples/frisian.md

sayings.text: Frisia pours neither oil nor wine.
sayings.source: Alcuin, poem to his friends on the Rhine (Carmen 4), our rendering as in peoples/frisian.md

sayings.text: I will swear alone. You, if you dare, deny my oath and fight me.
sayings.source: Lex Frisionum XI.3, our rendering from the Latin

sayings.text: A harper's hand, a goldsmith's hand, a weaving woman's hand: a quarter dearer than the rest of them.
sayings.source: Lex Frisionum, Additio III (the hand of a harper, a goldsmith or a woman who makes fresum), turned as a saying

sayings.text: On Sunday the sheep may eat. The shepherd may watch. Twelve shillings if he does more.
sayings.source: Lex Frisionum XVIII (servile work on Sunday costs 12 solidi beyond the Lauwers, 4 elsewhere), turned as a joke in the period's manner

sayings.text: The marsh has three harvests: wool, cheese, and whatever the tide leaves.
Pull a man out of the water and the law owes you four shillings. Push him in first and it is still four, if nobody saw.
sayings.source: Lex Frisionum (4 solidi for saving a man from the water), turned as a ferryman's joke; invented

sayings.text: I am told there are people who burn wood. I have seen a tree. I did not think it would catch.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, after Pliny, Natural History 16.1, on the coast people who burn dried mud (?)

easter_eggs.text: Look south from the mound: there is land where later ages will draw a bay. The Dollart has not happened yet; over the river lie peat and the Reiderland marsh.
Bant, the marsh island off the river mouth that was a whole district of Liudger's mission, is a little smaller each time the boat passes. The sea takes the last of it in 1780.

On the street a boy plays a flute a hand long, cut from a bone, and his mother fastens her bag with a bone toggle scored with three strokes crossed by an X: her house mark, she says, or else a tally she has forgotten.
easter_eggs.source: Fundchronik Emden 2001-2003 (a bone flute 11.5 cm long and a marked toggle from the Kirchstraße; 'medieval', probably later than 1066 (?))

easter_eggs.text: Horse bones lie in the midden with knife marks on them. Christians are not supposed to eat horse. About one bone in six says somebody did.
easter_eggs.source: Grimm 2010, chapter 7 (46 horse bones, 17 per cent butchered)

easter_eggs.text: A ploughman across the river turned up a soldier's bronze buckle and a spearhead of a make nobody knows. Bernlef says they are from the wars of kings before any he can name.
easter_eggs.source: de.wikipedia 'Bentumersiel' (Roman army gear in the marsh over the Ems)

easter_eggs.text: After 884 men from Norden say the archbishop prayed on a boulder while the Danes drowned, and that rain water from the hollows in it takes off warts.
easter_eggs.source: de.wikipedia 'Schlacht bei Norditi' (the local legend; Adam of Bremen counts 10,377 Danes dead)

easter_eggs.text: Cat skins are pegged out on a wall of the street. Ask, and the skinner says the cats were old. All of them.
The name on the pennies is AMVTHON, 'at the mouth of the A': the first time anyone wrote the place down, and they wrote it on money.
On the tide sand an old man will show where, in his grandfather's day, a man who robbed a shrine was led out at the ebb. He does not say what was done. He says the sea is a clean neighbour.
easter_eggs.source: Lex Frisionum, Additio XI ('this beyond the Lauwers')

unlocks.what: The knowledge of the Ems mouth: the west channel past Bant, the drying flats, the hour of slack water under the mound.
unlocks.how: Go out three tides with Folcger (three days and a penny a tide), or bring warning of the fleet in 810.
unlocks.gives: flag unlock_pilot_ems: no pilot is needed here and the way in is sure in fog and at night.

unlocks.what: Tetta's house keeps your goods and sells your cloth while you are away, and her daughters' daughters after her.
unlocks.how: Sell grain here at a fair price in a hungry year (the story 'Bread for cloth'), or carry the priest.
unlocks.gives: flag unlock_factor_emuthon: storage on the mound without rent, a free bed, and first choice of new cloth before Easter.

unlocks.what: A narrow plot fronting the street on the mound.
unlocks.how: Pay your part with the mound in 810, or pay for a stretch of the raising of the mound between about 850 and 920.
unlocks.gives: flag unlock_plot_emuthon: a house of your own here; goods winter dry; a voice at the tide sand.

unlocks.what: The count of Werl's word that your bales pass his post untolled (?).
unlocks.how: Stand by the count's pennies when the archbishop's man asks, 1047 to 1063 (the story 'Heriman's light pennies').
unlocks.gives: flag unlock_charter_emuthon: no toll at Emuthon; a cold welcome at the archbishop's markets over the river.

unlocks.what: Folcger's trust: a north-bound hull lying in the creek till moonset that will take what the king's law says may not leave the realm.
unlocks.how: Be known to Folcger (three visits), carry something for him without asking, and do not pay for the watch fire on the Nesse.
unlocks.gives: Blades and mail can be sold here for the Danish price less a third, with no toll man to pass (sets sw_ran_blades and sw_buyer_known); if the count's men ever ask Folcger, sw_marked.

unlocks.what: The knowledge of the light penny and the heavy.
unlocks.how: Test silver at the count's die between about 1020 and 1051 and at Daventre or Tiel in the same years.
unlocks.gives: The market panel shows, for each port, whether pennies are taken by count or by weight; about a fifth to be made on silver carried between them.
